findings.title: Body larger than maxBody is silently truncated and returned as success
findings.evidence: io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, maxBody)) stops at maxBody bytes with no error, so a server returning 1 MiB + 1 (or any larger payload, e.g. a normal JSON/HTML page) yields a partial byte slice and a nil error; callers cannot distinguish complete from truncated content and may parse/cache/persist corrupted data.
findings.recommendation: Read maxBody+1 bytes with io.LimitReader and return a distinct error (e.g. fmt.Errorf("body exceeds %d bytes", maxBody)) when len(body) > maxBody, or use http.MaxBytesReader semantics so oversize responses fail loudly. Add a test with a body of exactly maxBody and maxBody+1 that asserts an error, not a short success.

findings.title: Nil *http.Client from caller panics instead of returning an error
findings.evidence: Get accepts *http.Client and calls client.Do(req) with no nil check; a caller passing nil (a plausible mistake for someone expecting a default client, as with http.Get) gets a nil-pointer panic rather than a wrapped error.
findings.recommendation: Either default to http.DefaultClient when client == nil, or return an explicit error at entry (if client == nil { return nil, errors.New("nil http client") }).

findings.title: Non-200 response body closed without being drained
findings.evidence: Every non-200 exit path reaches defer resp.Body.Close() without reading the body, so the underlying connection cannot be reused; on repeated 4xx/5xx responses the client leaks connections until the transport pool churns.
findings.recommendation: Before returning the status error, drain a bounded amount of the body (e.g. io.CopyN(io.Discard, resp.Body, maxBody)) so the connection can return to the keep-alive pool.
